The company has suffered compounded sales growth of -14% over the last decade, a figure that has worsened significantly to -38% over the last three years and -56% over the trailing twelve months [E13, E15, E16]. This downward trajectory is starkly highlighted by the sector median sales growth of 12.9%, suggesting the company is failing to capture any industry tailwinds [E64]. Furthermore, the business is currently destroying shareholder value, evidenced by a negative ROE of -4.41% compared to a sector benchmark of 30.31% [E8]. Investors are paying a premium for this decline, as the stock trades at a price-to-book ratio of 3.87x, which is higher than the sector benchmark of 3.77x [E1, E6]. Conceded: the company’s ROA of -2.85% is significantly better than the sector benchmark of -171.35% [E7]. Given the lack of dividend yield, there is no income-based justification for holding this asset while the core business continues to shrink [E3].

Shiva Suitings Ltd presents a deeply troubled financial profile characterised by severe, accelerating top-line collapse across every measured timeframe, including a devastating compounded sales growth of -56% over the trailing twelve months [E16]. This contraction deepens further when looking at the 3-year (-38%), 5-year (-21%), and 10-year (-14%) horizons [E13, E14, E15], confirming a long-term structural decay that severely lags the broader sector median sales growth of 12.9% [E64]. The company is actively destroying shareholder capital, evidenced by a negative return on equity of -4.41% which completely misses the sector benchmark of 30.31% [E8], and a negative price-to-earnings multiple of -86.79x [E5]. Compounding these fundamental losses, the stock offers zero income return with a 0.00% dividend yield [E3], leaving investors uncompensated for holding a loss-making enterprise. Despite these overwhelming operational headwinds, the valuation remains entirely disconnected from reality, demanding a price-to-book ratio of 3.87x against a book value of just ₹ 12.8 [E1] and trading near the upper bound at 78% of its 52-week range [E4]. Conceded: the company's return on assets of -2.85% outperforms the extreme distress seen in the wider sector benchmark of -171.35% [E7].
